The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. The demonstrations also showed that the rule applies across outline colors; color selection followed frame dimensions, not the perimeter color. This is a pattern to test, not a universal ARC convention.\n\nThe test instance used the same rule: fill the interiors of the five complete rectangles, use 7 for the 3x3 and 3x4 frames, and 2 for the 4x4 and 6x6 frames. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN"}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. The transformation may add an auxiliary color (often 2) into selected background cells on the rectangle perimeter while leaving all interior cells and original markers intact. Do not assume the entire frame is uniformly filled: several demonstrations can preserve some perimeter gaps and fill others according to a repeating positional pattern.\n\n## Analysis method\n\n1. Compare input/output coordinates only on its perimeter; explicitly record original markers, added cells, and unchanged background cells, separately for top, bottom, left, and right edges.\n3. Test periodic selectors such as alternating positions, parity relative to an endpoint, or parity of row/column index. Use multiple differently sized examples to determine whether alternation resets at each edge/corner or continues around the full perimeter.\n4. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. The demonstrations also showed that the rule applies across outline colors; color selection followed frame dimensions, not the perimeter color. This is a pattern to test, not a universal ARC convention.\n\nThe test instance used the same rule: fill the interiors of the five complete rectangles, use 7 for the 3x3 and 3x4 frames, and 2 for the 4x4 and 6x6 frames. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN"}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. # Continual-ARC puzzle solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid instances in streamed evaluations where each instance is isolated, demos can be requested, and actions have explicit costs.

## Interaction contract

1. Read the current task, input grid, demo/attempt caps, and all feedback before acting. Treat each instance independently and rely only on its current conversation.
2. Every turn requires exactly one supported action. End with one JSON object: `{"action":"submit","grid":[...]}`, `{"action":"request_demos"}`, or (only when the instance is over) `{"action":"finish"}`. No commentary or extra JSON.
3. Preserve grid dimensions, row order, and all cells not changed by the inferred rule. Entries must be integer colors 0–9.
4. Optimize expected score: demos and wrong submissions cost 1 each; an unsolved instance costs the full budget. Request a demo when it can distinguish plausible rules; submit when the rule is adequately supported. Respect caps.

## Inference workflow

1. **Inventory the grid:** dimensions, background, salient colors, counts and coordinates, alignments, partitions, and symmetry.
2. **Compare examples cell-by-cell:** distinguish unchanged, recolored, added, and removed cells. Check whether original markers remain and whether new cells use a distinct color.
3. **Test simple global rules first:** row/column spans, consecutive-marker connections, rays, bounding boxes, object counts, shape completion, symmetry, and color replacement. For large grids, use a compact script rather than visual transcription alone.
4. **Use demos contrastively:** find a rule explaining all examples, including untouched cells and boundaries. A second example with different marker placement can discriminate row/column interpolation from object-specific or one-axis rules.
5. **State the exact rule internally:** eligible markers, axes, endpoints, consecutive vs. outermost pairs, fill color, and preservation of originals.
6. **Apply mechanically:** detect endpoints from the original grid, not from newly filled cells, unless iterative propagation is evidenced. Verify dimensions and preservation, then manually inspect representative rows and columns.
7. **Return only the required action JSON.**

## Pitfalls

- Do not infer a rule from one salient cluster if examples indicate a global transformation.
- Do not let newly filled cells become endpoints by accident.
- Do not overwrite marker endpoints or background indiscriminately.
- Test both row and column behavior independently; a line-filling rule may use both axes.
- Avoid no-op tool probes and narration. Use tools when they materially help derive or validate a large output.
- Do not stop at a plausible transformation: compare it against every demo, including unchanged regions, before submitting.

## Reference notes

- `references/sparse-line-interpolation.md` summarizes a validated example where gaps between consecutive marker cells are filled along rows and columns while preserving endpoints.

# Demo interpretation and action selection for streamed ARC

Use this class-level companion workflow when solving isolated ARC instances with costly demonstrations, limited attempts, and one-action-per-turn output requirements.

## Procedure

1. **Honor the interaction contract first.** Read the task, caps, test grid, and latest feedback. Return exactly one supported JSON action each turn; do not add explanation to a response whose protocol requires action-only output.
2. **Analyze before requesting.** For every demo, compare input and output cell by cell. Record all edits and salient unchanged regions. Separate the transformation operation from its selector: which object or region, what trigger, direction/geometry, and color mapping.
3. **Maintain a small hypothesis ledger.** Keep only materially different rules consistent with all examples. State how each predicts the test output. Negative evidence—similar structures left untouched—is as important as edited cells.
4. **Make each demo contrastive.** Request another only when you can name the unresolved distinction, identify test cells where candidate rules diverge, and explain what kind of example could discriminate them. Do not request reflexively after every result.
5. **Choose an action by expected value.** Demos and wrong submissions have costs; submit once the rule is adequately supported, and avoid a guess when a targeted demo can resolve a consequential ambiguity. Respect demo and attempt caps.
6. **Construct and validate mechanically.** Apply the chosen rule to the original test grid, preserve unsupported cells, and check dimensions, row widths, color range, and exact changed coordinates before submitting.
7. **After incorrect feedback, reject the whole candidate explanation.** Revisit the selector and trigger as well as the operation; never retry an identical or cosmetic variant without new evidence.

## Pitfalls

- A demo arriving does not itself imply another demo is needed: analyze its information before choosing the next action.
- Do not use repeated reference loading or narrated internal exploration as a substitute for comparing examples; load only the specific reference relevant to the unresolved question.
- Do not infer a broad rule from the most salient region while ignoring preserved counterexamples.

## Related references

For detailed ledger and contrastive-demo tactics, see `references/demo-diff-and-hypothesis-ledger.md` and `references/contrastive-demo-budgeting.md` in the `continual-arc` skill. For action-only output discipline, see `references/stream-action-discipline.md` there as well.

# Scale-changing ARC demo audit

Use this class-level companion when ARC demonstrations reduce, expand, crop, or otherwise change grid dimensions. Check representation and scale before transferring a cellwise transformation.

## Procedure

1. Record every demo's input and output dimensions before inspecting its motif. Look for consistent ratios, tile or block sizes, repeated lattice periods, and whether output bounds correspond to the count of complete or partial regions.
2. If the output is smaller, map candidate output cells to fixed-size input blocks or repeated panels. Test plausible summaries—foreground-only mode, all-color mode, marker sampling, or panel extraction—against every output cell in every demo. Explain background-only blocks too.
3. Audit boundaries and remainders explicitly. Input dimensions need not divide evenly; determine whether trailing partial blocks are discarded, included, or handled specially. The proposed rule must explain the output dimensions as well as cell values.
4. Separate the scale/representation rule from the content selector. Repeated background lattices with sparse unusual-color markers may encode a compact categorical grid; stripes that resemble lines do not by themselves support row/column filling.
5. Transfer only a candidate that explains all demos, including unchanged areas and every output cell. Construct the test output at the inferred dimensions and validate its shape and values.

- In action-only evaluations, return exactly one required JSON action per turn, with no explanation around it.

{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/rectangular-frame-inference.md", "content": "# Rectangular frame inference from sparse boundary markers

## Pattern

Several demos can reveal that sparse markers form parts of the boundary of a rectangle, with missing boundary cells painted in a third color. The rectangle is not necessarily the tight bounding box of *all* markers: unrelated internal or external markers may exist, and corner/boundary groups may identify a subset of the full marker set.

## Recovery procedure

1. Inventory marker coordinates by row and column. Look for rows with multiple markers suggesting horizontal boundary segments, and columns with repeated markers suggesting vertical sides.
2. Separate candidate boundary markers from unrelated interior markers. Check whether a proposed rectangle's opposite sides have repeated/similar support and whether its horizontal boundary rows contain contiguous marker runs or aligned endpoints.
3. Infer each of the four bounds independently from the demonstrated structure; do not use the global marker bounding box by default. A stray marker may extend beyond a true frame or sit inside it.
4. Fill only missing cells on the supported perimeter, preserving all original markers and the interior/background. Do not simultaneously apply generic row/column interpolation unless the output demos establish that rule independently.
5. Before submission, verify candidate perimeter against every demo: list exactly which cells changed, confirm all expected boundary gaps were filled, and confirm no unsupported boundary line or internal gap was altered.
6. On a rejected perimeter candidate, do not merely adjust one bound speculatively. Revisit the selector: determine which subset of markers forms the frame, whether it is one rectangle or multiple, and whether some markers are unrelated noise. With demos exhausted, submit a single distinct candidate only when its boundaries are supported by visible structure.

## Pitfalls

- A global bounding-box frame can be wrong when one marker lies outside or inside the actual frame.
- Interpolation between every consecutive marker in rows and columns is a separate rule; do not combine it with frame completion without evidence.
- Repeated demo requests without extracting exact changed and unchanged cells waste budget and do not resolve selector ambiguity.
- Keep coordinates zero-based internally or state a consistent one-based convention; audit row/column orientation when transferring from examples to test.

This is a hypothesis pattern, not a universal rule. Treat multiple rectangles, nested frames, and noise as live alternatives until the examples disambiguate them.

## Session note

In one instance, demos repeatedly showed a rectangle-like wireframe completed with color 2, while sparse 9/7/1 markers varied in dimensions and included interior markers. A naive global bounding-box perimeter and broad row/column interpolation both failed. The key lesson is selector caution: the demos supported frame completion in their small structures but did not justify treating every marker in a large test as a perimeter endpoint. Prefer another targeted demo if available; after the cap, avoid submitting the rejected global bbox again and identify a credible marker subset before constructing output.

A recurring frame task may contain several hollow, axis-aligned rectangular outlines with different colors and sizes. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.

1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.

3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.

## Validated example pattern

In one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. This is a pattern to test, not a universal ARC convention.

The test instance used the same rule: fill the interiors of the five complete rectangles, use 7 for the 3x3 and 3x4 frames, and 2 for the 4x4 and 6x6 frames. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.

## Pitfalls

- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.
- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.
- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.
- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.

# Scale-changing ARC demo audit

Use this class-level companion when ARC demonstrations reduce, expand, crop, or otherwise change grid dimensions. Check representation and scale before transferring a cellwise transformation.

## Procedure

1. Record every demo's input and output dimensions before inspecting its motif. Look for consistent ratios, tile or block sizes, repeated lattice periods, and whether output bounds correspond to the count of complete or partial regions.
2. If the output is smaller, map candidate output cells to fixed-size input blocks or repeated panels. Test plausible summaries—foreground-only mode, all-color mode, marker sampling, or panel extraction—against every output cell in every demo. Explain background-only blocks too.
3. Audit boundaries and remainders explicitly. Input dimensions need not divide evenly; determine whether trailing partial blocks are discarded, included, or handled specially. The proposed rule must explain the output dimensions as well as cell values.
4. Separate the scale/representation rule from the content selector. Repeated background lattices with sparse unusual-color markers may encode a compact categorical grid; stripes that resemble lines do not by themselves support row/column filling.
5. Transfer only a candidate that explains all demos, including unchanged areas and every output cell. Construct the test output at the inferred dimensions and validate its shape and values.
6. In costly streamed tasks, request a demo only when surviving rules differ at identified test cells and a possible contrast can resolve that difference. After rejection, revisit scale, aggregation, selector, and boundaries—not just one coordinate. If the user says to decide from current evidence or a turn was interrupted for budget, submit the best-supported candidate immediately rather than prolonging exploration.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume input and output dimensions match when demonstrations consistently show scale changes.
- Do not select a block-mode or downsampling rule from visual plausibility alone; validate it cell-by-cell, including empty blocks and edges.
- Do not infer unrestricted line filling from a repeated carrier pattern without proving which cells encode output values.
- In action-only evaluations, return exactly one required JSON action per turn, with no explanation around it.

For general demo comparison and costly action selection, also follow `continual-arc-demo-discipline`.

The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. The demonstrations also showed that the rule applies across outline colors; color selection followed frame dimensions, not the perimeter color. This is a pattern to test, not a universal ARC convention.\n\nThe test instance used the same rule: fill the interiors of the five complete rectangles, use 7 for the 3x3 and 3x4 frames, and 2 for the 4x4 and 6x6 frames. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN"}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN"}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. The demonstrations also showed that the rule applies across outline colors; color selection followed frame dimensions, not the perimeter color. This is a pattern to test, not a universal ARC convention.\n\nThe test instance used the same rule: fill the interiors of the five complete rectangles, use 7 for the 3x3 and 3x4 frames, and 2 for the 4x4 and 6x6 frames. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN", "anchor": true}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. Compute the bounding rectangle of the original markers (min/max row and column).\n2. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. The demonstrations also showed that the rule applies across outline colors; color selection followed frame dimensions, not the perimeter color. This is a pattern to test, not a universal ARC convention.\n\nThe test instance used the same rule: fill the interiors of the five complete rectangles, use 7 for the 3x3 and 3x4 frames, and 2 for the 4x4 and 6x6 frames. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN", "anchor": true}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. # Continual-ARC puzzle solving

Use this skill for ARC-style grid instances in streamed evaluations where each instance is isolated, demos can be requested, and actions have explicit costs.

## Interaction contract

1. Read the current task, input grid, demo/attempt caps, and all feedback before acting. Treat each instance independently and rely only on its current conversation.
2. Every turn requires exactly one supported action. End with one JSON object: `{"action":"submit","grid":[...]}`, `{"action":"request_demos"}`, or (only when the instance is over) `{"action":"finish"}`. No commentary or extra JSON.
3. Preserve grid dimensions, row order, and all cells not changed by the inferred rule. Entries must be integer colors 0–9.
4. Optimize expected score: demos and wrong submissions cost 1 each; an unsolved instance costs the full budget. Request a demo when it can distinguish plausible rules; submit when the rule is adequately supported. Respect caps.

## Inference workflow

1. **Inventory the grid:** dimensions, background, salient colors, counts and coordinates, alignments, partitions, and symmetry.
2. **Compare examples cell-by-cell:** distinguish unchanged, recolored, added, and removed cells. Check whether original markers remain and whether new cells use a distinct color.
3. **Test simple global rules first:** row/column spans, consecutive-marker connections, rays, bounding boxes, object counts, shape completion, symmetry, and color replacement. For large grids, use a compact script rather than visual transcription alone.
4. **Use demos contrastively:** find a rule explaining all examples, including untouched cells and boundaries. A second example with different marker placement can discriminate row/column interpolation from object-specific or one-axis rules.
5. **State the exact rule internally:** eligible markers, axes, endpoints, consecutive vs. outermost pairs, fill color, and preservation of originals.
6. **Apply mechanically:** detect endpoints from the original grid, not from newly filled cells, unless iterative propagation is evidenced. Verify dimensions and preservation, then manually inspect representative rows and columns.
7. **Return only the required action JSON.**

## Pitfalls

- Do not infer a rule from one salient cluster if examples indicate a global transformation.
- Do not let newly filled cells become endpoints by accident.
- Do not overwrite marker endpoints or background indiscriminately.
- Test both row and column behavior independently; a line-filling rule may use both axes.
- Avoid no-op tool probes and narration. Use tools when they materially help derive or validate a large output.
- Do not stop at a plausible transformation: compare it against every demo, including unchanged regions, before submitting.

## Reference notes

- `references/sparse-line-interpolation.md` summarizes a validated example where gaps between consecutive marker cells are filled along rows and columns while preserving endpoints.

# Scale-changing ARC demo audit

Use this class-level companion when ARC demonstrations reduce, expand, crop, or otherwise change grid dimensions. Check representation and scale before transferring a cellwise transformation.

## Procedure

1. Record every demo's input and output dimensions before inspecting its motif. Look for consistent ratios, tile or block sizes, repeated lattice periods, and whether output bounds correspond to the count of complete or partial regions.
2. If the output is smaller, map candidate output cells to fixed-size input blocks or repeated panels. Test plausible summaries—foreground-only mode, all-color mode, marker sampling, or panel extraction—against every output cell in every demo. Explain background-only blocks too.
3. Audit boundaries and remainders explicitly. Input dimensions need not divide evenly; determine whether trailing partial blocks are discarded, included, or handled specially. The proposed rule must explain the output dimensions as well as cell values.
4. Separate the scale/representation rule from the content selector. Repeated background lattices with sparse unusual-color markers may encode a compact categorical grid; stripes that resemble lines do not by themselves support row/column filling.
5. Transfer only a candidate that explains all demos, including unchanged areas and every output cell. Construct the test output at the inferred dimensions and validate its shape and values.
6. In costly streamed tasks, request a demo only when surviving rules differ at identified test cells and a possible contrast can resolve that difference. After rejection, revisit scale, aggregation, selector, and boundaries—not just one coordinate. If the user says to decide from current evidence or a turn was interrupted for budget, submit the best-supported candidate immediately rather than prolonging exploration.

## Pitfalls

- Do not assume input and output dimensions match when demonstrations consistently show scale changes.
- Do not select a block-mode or downsampling rule from visual plausibility alone; validate it cell-by-cell, including empty blocks and edges.
- Do not infer unrestricted line filling from a repeated carrier pattern without proving which cells encode output values.
- In action-only evaluations, return exactly one required JSON action per turn, with no explanation around it.

For general demo comparison and costly action selection, also follow `continual-arc-demo-discipline`.

# Demo interpretation and action selection for streamed ARC

Use this class-level companion workflow when solving isolated ARC instances with costly demonstrations, limited attempts, and one-action-per-turn output requirements.

## Procedure

1. **Honor the interaction contract first.** Read the task, caps, test grid, and latest feedback. Return exactly one supported JSON action each turn; do not add explanation to a response whose protocol requires action-only output.
2. **Analyze before requesting.** For every demo, compare input and output cell by cell. Record all edits and salient unchanged regions. Separate the transformation operation from its selector: which object or region, what trigger, direction/geometry, and color mapping.
3. **Maintain a small hypothesis ledger.** Keep only materially different rules consistent with all examples. State how each predicts the test output. Negative evidence—similar structures left untouched—is as important as edited cells.
4. **Make each demo contrastive.** Request another only when you can name the unresolved distinction, identify test cells where candidate rules diverge, and explain what kind of example could discriminate them. Do not request reflexively after every result.
5. **Choose an action by expected value.** Demos and wrong submissions have costs; submit once the rule is adequately supported, and avoid a guess when a targeted demo can resolve a consequential ambiguity. Respect demo and attempt caps.
6. **Construct and validate mechanically.** Apply the chosen rule to the original test grid, preserve unsupported cells, and check dimensions, row widths, color range, and exact changed coordinates before submitting.
7. **After incorrect feedback, reject the whole candidate explanation.** Revisit the selector and trigger as well as the operation; never retry an identical or cosmetic variant without new evidence.

The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN"}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7. Preserve all perimeters and other cells.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Do not infer a single fill color from the first framed object.\n- Do not conflate parity of area with parity of both dimensions; log width and height separately.\n- Do not fill plausible but unclosed or partial shapes without demo evidence.\n- Do not recolor frame edges when examples only add interior cells.\n", "file_type": ".md", "_source_path": "/home/USER/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/stage1/H-hermes-luna6-high-rnd0/frozen/seen/play/users/u036/system/state/hermes/skills/reasoning/continual-arc/references/frame-interior-parity-selection.md"}", "timestamp": 1792641288.8333542, "tool_name": "skill_view", "tool_call_id": "call_g3u3gJPyit3OpZhEdFMsrUSN"}, {"id": 9926, "role": "tool", "content": "{"success": true, "name": "continual-arc", "file": "references/perimeter-completion-and-color-parity.md", "content": "# Perimeter completion with selective gaps\n\nA sparse field can encode a rectangle through marker cells placed on its boundary. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. The operation and the color selector should be inferred separately.\n\n## Procedure\n\n1. Detect each closed rectangular frame from its complete perimeter; do not treat isolated L-shapes or open outlines as frames.\n2. Fill only the strict interior, preserving the original perimeter and all unrelated cells.\n3. Compare every framed object across demos. Record outer height and width, strict-interior dimensions, input perimeter color, and observed fill color. Look for a selector based on dimensions or parity rather than assuming all interiors share one fill color.\n4. Treat non-square frames as informative tests. A rule like “both outer dimensions even selects color 2; otherwise color 7” fits a useful contrastive pattern, but must be verified against all demos before transfer.\n5. Check non-frames and incomplete shapes as negative evidence, then mechanically verify the output bounds, interior cells, and preservation of borders.\n\n## Validated example pattern\n\nIn one demonstrated task, complete rectangles with even-by-even outer dimensions (4x4 and 6x6) had their interiors filled with 2, while rectangles whose outer dimensions were not both even—including odd squares and a 4x3 rectangle—were filled with 7.
